title: Teachers and AI: Understanding the factors influencing AI integration in K–12 education
extended_summary:
This paper examines the psychological and pedagogical factors that shape K–12 teachers’ readiness to integrate artificial intelligence into instruction. The study asks what helps or hinders teachers’ adoption of AI, with particular attention to efficiency, student engagement, curriculum alignment, ethics, and cultural fit.

The researchers used an exploratory qualitative design in a professional development context at a private school in Türkiye. Sixty-six teachers from 11 disciplines participated in a 14-week AI-in-education course within a Digital Learning Academy. Data came from online discussion forums and AI-supported learning-activity design tasks, and were analyzed inductively using thematic analysis.

Findings showed that teachers viewed AI positively for saving time, supporting lesson planning, enabling differentiated instruction, and increasing interactivity and personalization. ChatGPT and MagicSchool were frequently mentioned as useful tools. At the same time, teachers identified barriers including technical problems, limited devices, workload, curriculum misalignment, language and cultural mismatch, privacy/security concerns, risks of plagiarism, and worries that students could become less creative or overly reliant on AI. The authors conclude that AI can support teaching, but successful integration requires better infrastructure, targeted teacher support, and stronger ethical and curricular alignment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM tool that produces human-like text responses and supports content generation, drafting, and interactive prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers in AI-supported lesson/activity design and referenced as a commonly used classroom AI tool for lesson planning, quiz/story creation, and other instructional tasks.

identified_tools.name: MagicSchool
identified_tools.description: A teacher-facing generative AI platform offering multiple tools for lesson planning, content creation, student support, and classroom productivity.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers as an AI tool in designed activities and discussed as a preferred tool for lesson planning, content generation, adaptation, and support.

identified_tools.name: Canva
identified_tools.description: A design and content-creation platform used for generating visual materials, presentations, and learning resources.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned as an AI-supported tool used in designed learning activities, especially for visual design and differentiated instruction.

identified_tools.name: Gamma
identified_tools.description: An AI-powered presentation/content generation tool used to quickly create slide decks and other instructional materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers for presentation creation in lesson activities and cited as a preferred tool for quickly preparing presentation files.

identified_tools.name: Character.ai
identified_tools.description: A generative AI character-chat platform that enables users to create and interact with AI personas for conversation and learning tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in classroom activities for creating characters, discussions, and reflective or creative learning tasks.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's generative AI chatbot/model family for conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Referenced in the literature review as part of the broader evolution of LLMs; also appears in the paper's discussion of AI tools by way of Google's Bard/Gemini family normalization.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative study with 66 teachers from one private school, so the evidence is descriptive and context-specific rather than causal. It provides useful implementation insight but no experimental effect estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived benefits and barriers, including concerns about curriculum mismatch, privacy, creativity loss, and inaccurate content, but does not measure impact on learning outcomes. Any positive impact is reported only as teacher perception, so overall impact remains unclear.
